picked.t: Vietnam set to overtake Southeast Asia's largest economy in GDP per capita this year
picked.body: The figures, from the IMF's October World Economic Outlook, put Vietnam's nominal output per person 8.9% above last year's level and nearly double what it was a decade earlier. Vietnam trailed Indonesia by about $250 last year, IMF estimates show, and the fund's April outlook had still projected Indonesia staying ahead in 2026. The new projections would make Vietnam fifth among ASEAN members, behind Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Thailand. The IMF expects it to keep its lead over Indonesia in 2027, at $5,659 against $5,550. Indonesia remains Southeast Asia's largest economy by far. With nearly three times Vietnam's population of just over 100 million, its GDP is projected at $1.48 trillion this year, against Vietnam's $542 billion. Nikkei Asia linked the shift to Vietnam's growing role in high-tech manufacturing of semiconductors and electronics, noting that Taiwan's Foxconn is expanding production there. South Korea's Samsung Electronics makes smartphones and other electronics for export at its northern Vietnamese factories. Vietnam's economy grew 9.95% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in four years. The government's public investment push is also supporting growth, Mai Fujita, a senior research fellow at Japan's Institute of Developing Economies, told Nikkei Asia . Vietnam plans to spend VND1.014 quadrillion ($39.3 billion) on public investment this year, with roads, airports and other infrastructure under construction nationwide. Indonesia's growth, by contrast, has hovered around 5%. The IMF forecasts 5.1% for the country this year, against 8.4% for Vietnam. Vietnam is targeting growth of at least 10% this year and aims to lift GDP per capita to about $8,500 by 2030, roughly Thailand's level today. Fujita said Vietnam also needs to pursue long-term growth by developing human resources and technology, alongside the infrastructure spending that lifts growth in the short term.

picked.t: The Coca-Cola Foundation, IUCN seek business opportunities in ecosystem restoration
picked.body: The Coca-Cola Foundation (TCCF) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) presented business opportunities linked to ecosystem restoration at the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum in Ho Chi Minh City on Oct. 27. At a panel discussion titled "Turning ecosystem restoration into scalable business opportunities," the organizations showcased nature-based solutions that combine conservation with economic activities in the Mekong Delta. The discussion, held at the Rising Star Arena – Technology and Innovation Showcase, brought together stakeholders to explore ways to attract investment and generate income for local communities through restoration projects. The Mekong Delta faces coastal erosion, mangrove loss, disrupted seasonal flooding, excessive groundwater extraction and land subsidence, threatening agricultural production and local livelihoods. Since 2017, TCCF, the philanthropic arm of The Coca-Cola Company, has provided more than US$1.8 million to support IUCN projects linking ecosystem restoration with agriculture and market opportunities. One initiative promotes flood-based agriculture, combining lotus cultivation, aquaculture and tourism as alternatives to a third annual rice crop. Farmers can use seasonal floodwaters to produce lotus-based food, fiber, textiles and artwork, while generating income from aquaculture and tourism. Another model combines mangrove restoration with integrated multi-trophic aquaculture and recirculating aquaculture systems (IMTA-RAS). It integrates conservation with aquaculture technology to maintain production, improve water-use efficiency and quality, and strengthen coastal resilience. The organizations said scaling up these models would require commercially viable projects, measurable outcomes, partnerships and access to finance. Blended finance, which combines public and commercial funding, could help attract investment. Public funding can support project preparation, technical assistance, implementation and monitoring, while private capital can finance investments and expansion. IUCN and TCCF said they aimed to strengthen cooperation among businesses, public agencies and other stakeholders to mobilize resources for sustainable development in the Mekong Delta. TCCF also supports other environmental initiatives in Vietnam. Since 2007, it has worked with WWF-Viet Nam on biodiversity conservation and natural water regulation at Tram Chim National Park, committing an additional $500,000 for 2024–2027. The foundation also partners with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) on the Ending Plastic Waste Innovation Programme, which supports local waste management solutions. The program has incubated and accelerated 11 innovation projects and supported efforts to prevent or recycle more than 750 tonnes of plastic waste, while seeking to improve livelihoods for waste management workers.

picked.t: Company of Southeast Asia’s richest man posts first $1B quarterly profit
picked.body: Vietnam’s largest listed company saw revenue almost quadruple year-on-year to VND150.58 trillion, according to the company’s financial report. As in the first two quarters, real estate generated the largest share of revenue, at nearly VND98.5 trillion, or more than 65% of the total. By September-end, Vingroup held nearly VND107 trillion in cash and bank deposits. During the period, it also raised about $2.3 billion through bond issuance, the sale of preferred shares and syndicated loans from international investors. Since 2025, Vingroup has expanded into power and infrastructure, alongside traditional businesses including real estate, industrial manufacturing and technology. Real estate, however, remains the main growth driver for the conglomerate led by billionaire Vuong. VNDirect Securities estimates that real estate will remain Vingroup’s mainstay, contributing at least 50% of its total revenue and profit over the next five years. Meanwhile, its electric vehicle, infrastructure and energy businesses are expected to expand rapidly, raising their combined share of the group’s revenue to 30%–40% over the long term. This year, Vuong’s conglomerate is developing a series of major projects across the country. In real estate, it is building several urban areas spanning thousands of hectares, including projects in Quang Ninh, Hanoi and HCMC. In infrastructure, Vingroup, through its subsidiaries, is involved in engineering, procurement and construction contracts for five urban railway lines in Hanoi, with a total value of about $49 billion. Vuong, chairman of Vingroup, is the richest man in Southeast Asia with $37.7 billion in net worth, according to real-time data by Forbes.

picked.t: Moroccan student's journey from knowing only the local words for 'hello' to becoming Vietnam's top maritime navigation graduate
picked.body: A photograph of 23-year-old Moroccan student Hiba Faradji beaming as she accepted a top graduate award at Vietnam Maritime University in August quickly went viral across social media. However, behind this picture-perfect moment of triumph lies a deeply turbulent and emotionally taxing journey that nearly derailed her academic dreams. Her story began at the age of 18, when Faradji left her coastal hometown of Tangier, Morocco. Armed with a prestigious medical scholarship, she relocated to France to begin her studies at the renowned Sorbonne University in Paris. Unfortunately, her arrival coincided with the sudden, global outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic. The unprecedented health crisis immediately threw her academic plans into chaos. Her coursework became increasingly difficult to manage, and her living situation grew highly unstable. Forced to repeatedly stay with acquaintances far from the university campus, Faradji simultaneously battled a series of personal setbacks. After enduring eight months of stress and isolation, the overwhelmed student made the difficult decision to abandon her medical studies entirely and return to Morocco, facing a highly uncertain future. Deeply discouraged by the setback, Faradji isolated herself at home for nearly seven months. The once-outgoing student found herself battling depression, withdrawing completely from the outside world and plagued by a constant fear of being controlled by others. As her mental health gradually stabilized, she resumed her search for international education programs. However, she quickly faced a new wave of obstacles, enduring repeated rejections from universities in both Spain and South Korea. In late 2022, just as she was feeling entirely out of options, a lifeline emerged. Faradji stumbled upon an announcement for four full academic scholarships being offered by the Vietnam Maritime University. Seeking a way out of her predicament, she applied for the university’s bachelor’s program in maritime navigation, encouraged by the full scholarship. Her family supported the decision, and a close friend of her mother even helped pay for her plane ticket. "I had very little time to prepare or learn about Vietnam. I just thought Hai Phong might be similar to my hometown, a coastal city that was neither too big nor too remote," Faradji recalled. Her first day in Vietnam was yet another memorable experience. In February 2023, Faradji arrived at Hanoi's Noi Bai International Airport just before the Lunar New Year, Vietnam's largest national holiday and the most important occasion for family reunion. With passenger buses practically unavailable during the peak travel season, she had little choice but to spend VND2.5 million (US$97), half the total cash she was carrying along at that moment, on a direct taxi to Hai Phong. She arrived to find her cold dormitory completely deserted, as local students had already left for their hometowns for the holiday, leaving her on the verge of tears and wishing she could fly straight back home. As her parents called to check on her, Faradji pulled herself together and told herself she had to keep going. Challenges continued Although she had a strong command of English and French, Faradji found her coursework "quite difficult" because of the specialized terminology and calculations involved. "Math has never been my strength, while Ship Stability is highly detailed and technical. It was so difficult that I could not cover the entire curriculum in just two semesters," she said. To overcome difficulties, she spent considerable time studying independently at home to keep up. She identified her biggest challenges as the psychological wounds she had carried from Paris, differences in daily life in a new environment, and being one of the few female students in a predominantly male department. As a Muslim, Faradji strictly avoids pork. During her first three months in Hai Phong, before becoming accustomed to local cuisine, she subsisted largely on nuts and dried foods sent by her mother. Poor nutrition caused her to lose 4 kg and suffer from prolonged insomnia. Language was another obstacle. Initially, she knew only one Vietnamese phrase: "xin chao," meaning "hello." After five months of basic Vietnamese lessons, combined with observing and imitating the people around her, she gradually became more confident. A turning point came when Faradji joined an English club, where she befriended a student named Thuy, who invited her to stay with her family. This gave Faradji an opportunity to practice speaking Vietnamese in everyday situations. She eventually became familiar even with distinctive expressions and speech patterns used by people in Hai Phong. Once she settled into her studies, Faradji began supporting herself by taking part-time jobs and renting her own apartment. picked.t: Travel + Leisure, Lonely Planet recommend November visits to Ha Long
picked.body: November is among the recommended months to visit Ha Long Bay in northern Vietnam, according to international travel publications Travel + Leisure and Lonely Planet . In an article updated on Oct. 11, Travel + Leisure listed April, October and November as suitable months for cruising the UNESCO World Heritage Site, when weather is generally warm, sunny and dry. Lonely Planet also recommends October and November for visiting Ha Long Bay and neighboring Bai Tu Long Bay, citing mild temperatures and a greater likelihood of dry weather. The conditions are suitable for exploring the bay's limestone formations, caves and islands by boat or kayak. Travel + Leisure also recommends overnight cruises, which allow visitors to spend more time exploring the bay and see its scenery at different times of day. Trips typically include afternoon sightseeing, dinner on board and an overnight stay. Beyond cruises, visitors can explore attractions in Bai Chay, one of Ha Long's main tourism areas. Ha Long International Cruise Port, developed by Sun Group, serves cruise passengers and is close to hotels, restaurants and entertainment facilities. At Sun World Ha Long, the Queen Cable Car crosses the entrance to Cua Luc Bay, offering views of Bai Chay Bridge, the waterfront and surrounding urban areas. It connects to Ba Deo Hill, which features a Japanese-style garden with koi ponds, black pine trees and walking paths. Bai Chay also has dining and entertainment options for visitors in the evening. Vui-Fest Ha Long, in the Lighthouse area, features street food, shopping and entertainment, while Sun Bavaria Ha Long offers dining options for families and groups. For visitors seeking wellness activities, Quang Hanh offers hot-spring experiences amid a mountainous landscape. Hilton Quang Hanh Onsen Resort provides accommodation with private hot-spring bathing facilities, while the area's natural mineral springs offer an option for relaxation during the cooler months. With cruises, cable-car rides, dining venues and hot-spring facilities, Ha Long offers visitors several options for November trips. The recommendations from Travel + Leisure and Lonely Planet highlight the bay's seasonal conditions, while nearby attractions provide additional activities beyond sightseeing on the water.

picked.t: Vietnam lowers electricity price, first time in almost 20 years
picked.body: Average retail price is now at VND2,159.90 per kilowatt-hour, according to the Vietnam Electricity. This is the first decrease in the average electricity price in nearly 20 years, excluding five rounds of reductions in electricity bills and prices to support people and businesses affected by Covid-19. Between 2023 and 2025, electricity prices rose by 18.2% in four adjustments. The last increase was made in May 2025. Before those increases, electricity prices had remained unchanged for more than four years, from March 2019 to May 2023. EVN said the reduction followed a review of its operations and efforts to calculate and cut costs as much as possible. The adjustment is intended to support people and businesses, help stabilize the macroeconomy and ensure social welfare. At a National Assembly session on economic and social issues on the morning of Oct. 31, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang said the government had directed EVN to cut costs as much as possible to lower average retail electricity prices by about 2%. He said the electricity price reduction, together with a plan to cut the special consumption tax on gasoline to zero, would provide about 0.07 percentage points of additional room to control inflation and work toward the 4.5% target set by the National Assembly.

picked.t: Lonely Planet's 10 must-visit destinations in Vietnam have most bases covered
picked.body: Lonely Planet describes Vietnam as a destination offering a wide variety of rich experiences. The travel guide recently listed 10 top-rated spots across the country, ranging from cities and tropical islands to beaches and national parks. Hanoi: The ideal gateway for first-time visitors Every journey needs a starting point, and for first-time visitors to Vietnam, the capital city of Hanoi is the perfect place to begin. Beyond its accessible infrastructure, budget-friendly accommodations, world-class cuisine, and rich historical heritage, Hanoi serves as the gateway to iconic destinations such as Ha Long Bay and the renowned trekking routes of the northwest. The city offers an array of attractions and engaging activities. Whatever your itinerary looks like, sampling Hanoi's street food is a must. Insider tip: Grab a draught beer ( bia hoi ) at Ta Hien Street and explore the vibrant food stalls tucked along this famous alley. Photo by My Linh Phong Nha: hub for adventure As the world's largest cave, Son Doong is an awe-inspiring wonder. However, visitor slots are strictly limited and often booked years in advance. Beyond Son Doong, Phong Nha - Ke Bang National Park has countless other caverns waiting to be explored, where thrill-seekers can climb, squeeze through narrow passages, navigate underground rivers by boat, and rappel on ropes. Insider tip: Caves like Tu Lan, Phong Nha, Paradise (Thien Duong), and En offer more accessible price points. On these treks, campers pitch their tents on underground sandbars directly beneath massive sinkholes, illuminated by natural beams of sunlight streaming through the cavern openings. Photo by Jungle Boss Hue: historic destination As the former capital of the Nguyen Dynasty, Vietnam's last royal dynasty, Hue is steeped in imperial history despite suffering heavy damage due to wartime airstrikes. Though many original structures were destroyed, the grand legacy of the ancient capital endures within the Imperial Citadel and the Purple Forbidden City (Tu Cam Thanh). Just beyond the city center lie the royal tombs of Vietnam's former emperors, nestled amidst lush greenery along the Huong river. Another jewel of Hue's heritage is its royal cuisine, widely celebrated as the pinnacle of Vietnamese gastronomy. Don't miss out on trying a steaming bowl of spicy beef noodle soup bun bo Hue or a crispy savory pancake banh khoai . Insider tip: To beat the crowds at the royal tombs, rent a motorbike to explore at your own pace. And be sure to save time for a visit to the renowned Thien Mu pagoda. Photo by Quy Coc Tu Lan Ha Bay and Bai Tu Long Bay: ideal for boat cruises Beyond the world-famous Ha Long Bay, visitors can explore the equally stunning Lan Ha Bay and Bai Tu Long Bay aboard traditional wooden junk boats. You can also kayak through towering limestone karsts, hike forest trails on Cat Ba island, or unwind on the sandy shores of Co To island. The region is also packed with beaches and exceptional seafood restaurants. Insider tip: If you visit Cat Ba island, take time to trek the scenic trails of Cat Ba National Park with a local guide to fully appreciate its untouched nature. Photo by Pham Huy Trung Phu Quoc: haven for relaxation and family getaways Fringed by emerald-green waters and soft, powdery sands, Phu Quoc is the perfect spot to slow down and sip a cocktail as the sun sets. Long popular with both domestic and international travelers, the island offers a wealth of family-friendly attractions, including the VinWonders theme park and Sun World Hon Thom Nature Park. For a change of scenery, visitors can leave the bustling beach crowds behind to explore the dense forests of the island. Insider tip: Numerous airlines operate direct flights to Phu Quoc. Besides, foreign travelers can take advantage of a visa-free policy for stays of up to 30 days. Photo by Sun Group Hoi An: step back in time Once one of Asia’s important trading ports, attracting merchants from far-off lands such as Japan, Spain, and North America, Hoi An is a charming old town characterized by tightly packed shophouses, a centuries-old covered bridge, Chinese assembly halls, Buddhist pagodas, and Confucian temples. History, however, is only part of Hoi An's allure. Many travelers extend their stays for days to attend hands-on cooking classes with local chefs, mastering dishes like "white rose" dumplings ( banh bao banh vac ) and fresh spring rolls. Visitors also flock to the town's famous tailor shops, renowned for high-quality custom clothing at affordable prices. Insider tip: Stay at a homestay in Bho Hoong, a village inhabited by the Co Tu ethnic group. It offers a unique window into local indigenous culture and a peaceful retreat from the bustle of the town. Photo by NickM Ha Giang: authentic mountain experience If you want to explore the countryside without jostling through heavy tourist crowds, Ha Giang is the ideal destination.
